div.head: Pascoe's Progress: publishing and tourism at the turn of the 19th century
div.p: The career of Charles Eyre Pascoe (1843-1912), a now largely forgotten journalist and editor, is visible today almost exclusively through the lens of his publications: he does not seem to have kept a diary, and the facts of his personal life can only be gleaned from census and similar records. Most of his publications are now readily available in digital facsimile or print on demand, but have not to my knowledge been much studied, despite their evident appeal to the neo-Victorianist. Glimpses of his youth may be found in published memoirs of the Bostonian journalist community of the 1870s, but for his personal life during his heyday as a London editor, we have only his own accounts, somewhat obscured by the authorial persona he adopted. His style, derived ultimately (as one critical reviewer noted) from Carlyle, is seen perhaps at its most extreme in a curious 1893 work London's world's fair for 1893 and Great Social, Political, and Moral Exposition. The Spirit of the Age at a glance from which this image is taken. Pascoe is the slightly perplexed, but definitely respectable cove in a top hat on the left; the other faintly bohemian chap is the artist responsible for the picture, Fred Pegram. They are depicted trying to decide what copy they can deliver to the importunate messenger boy at right.

Who was the “Charles Eyre Pascoe” who put this work together?Though almost entirely forgotten today, a look at his short career may shed some light on some little-explored by-ways of the late Victorian writing business. For business it undeniably was.

He was born in Yeovil on the 22nd of June 1842, fifth son of Richard William Pascoe (1785-1869), a Captain with the rank of Brevet Major in the Royal Marines, and his wife Mary Ann, nee Hitchens (1808-1897). Young Charles was fortunate enough to get a free education at Christ’s Hospital, and seems to have done well, despite (according to his own reminiscence) frequently playing truant. In 1859, aged 18, he passed a “competative” examination qualifying him to work as a civil servant in the Admiralty, which he appears to have done for the next ten years.

In November 1869, his father died, leaving an estate of £5,000. It may be pure coincidence that in the same year Charles decided to take early retirement from the Civil Service, start his journalistic career, and get married. Jane Catherine Smith, the lucky girl, was three years younger than him. Her surname discourages research, but it’s possible she brought some money to complete whatever Charles inherited from his father. The marriage took place on the 30th August 1870 at St Michael’s Church in Pimlico and the happy couple moved into what is now a highly desirable address: 51 Cambridge Street. A daughter, Ethel Mary, was born in 1872 followed by a son Charles Corbett in 1876 and another daughter, Mary Agnes, in 1881.

An immigration record shows that Pascoe, accompanied by wife and baby Ethel, arrived in Boston on board the S.S. Hecla, on 23 September 1873. However, this was not his first transatlantic crossing. In December of 1872, following a dinner in honour of the explorer Henry Morton Stanley, he is named among the founder members of a Boston dining club called the Papyrus Club. In February of 1873, he signs a printed invitation from the Club as “Very respectfully yours, Chas E. PASCOE, Secretary.” From an article about the club in the Boston Herald of March 1888, we learn that “Pascoe was always called upon to sing “Guy Fawkes,” and was always ready to do it”. It seems clear that during his three years in the United States he established himself in the little community of Bostonian journalists. Much later, in 1906, he claimed “Five years after the close of the American Civil War, Mr. Pascoe went to America, at a time when popular feeling in the Northern States was still irritated and unfriendly towards England, and there became appointed Editor of Foreign Intelligence to the Boston Daily Globe—the only Englishman in that city then admitted to the staff of an American journal.” His appointment as “foreign correspondent” for the Boston Globe gave him an entree to that society, and a way of continuing his transatlantic connexion after he returned to England in 1874 -- in 1893, he remarks “Last year, I made the Atlantic passage for the tenth time.” It also laid the foundation for his life long love affair with American manners and culture.

His first publication was a pamphlet contrasting the effectiveness of American and British attempts to control public drunkenness: “The prohibitory law of Massachusetts versus the licensing law of England: with an account of the latter” . This 1874 pamphlet marks the first appearance of the narrative strategy which characterises much of his work: combining statistical detail with knowledgeable mediation, as a means of explaining the ways of John Bull to Cousin Jonathan, thus opening the latter’s eyes to the former’s distinguished and lengthy history.

In the same year, and also with a Boston imprint, appeared the first of many Guide Books: A London directory for American travellers for 1874: containing the fullest information, in the best form for reference, respecting all that is valuable in connection with a visit to London. Originally published by Lee and Shephards, this venture was successful enough to warrant several subsequent editions, both in Boston and in London, where the 5th edition appeared under the imprint of Simpkin Marshall & Co in 1876. It is a bravura cut-and-paste job, combining railway and steamer time tables with detailed advice on obtaining accomodation, nourishment and polite entertainment at a modest (but not insignificant) cost, and liberally sprinkled with advertisements. It constructs London life and in particular London society as spectacle for the visitor, long before the insights of Guy Debord. And it is of course the parent of Pascoe’s most successful publication, “London of To-day”.

In the Post Office directory for 1875, Pascoe’s London operation appears for the first time at its own address : 6A Vigo Street, just off Regent Street, where he is registered as “editor of Pascoe’s Guide for American Travellers, Boston & New York” Also registered at the same address were a tailor, a “financial agent”, a shirt maker, and a wine merchant: it is thus clearly a non-residential business address. Over the next decade Pascoe embarked on an ambitious programme of reference publishing.

In 1878 he published with Sampson Lowe the first of four works addressed at anxious parents. “A Practical Handbook to the Principal Schools of England” of which the Examiner remarked “This is an exceedingly useful work and one that was much wanted”, though it also remarks that “a little infusion of literary feeling would have done no harm” Pascoe seems to have taken this to heart for many of his subsequent reference works -- in particular but not exclusively the Guide Books -- are full of “literary feeling” and reminiscence.

In 1879, he complemented this survey of educational opportunity with Schools for girls and colleges for women : a handbook of female education chiefly designed for the use of persons of the upper middle class, which (according to the >Basingstoke and North Hampshire Gazette) attempted to answer the “perplexing question” “What to do with the girls?”, in particular girls whose parents are neither rich enough to send their offspring off to be educated with the aristocracy nor poor enough for them to benefit from the Board schools.

Pascoe, himself just such a parent, returns frequently to the plight of the respectable middle class, notably in his 1884 pamphlet Where shall I educate my son? A manual for parents of moderate means. As a natural sequel to these pedagogic works, in 1878 he published A Practical Handbook to the Principal Professions, which specifies in some detail the hurdles to be overcome by would-be members of the professions. These Handbooks all combine a certain amount of polemic with a plentiful supply of practical suggestions, price lists, and even (somewhat terrifying) sample examination papers.

In 1879, he published a rather different work with David Bogue. “The dramatic list; a record of the principal performances of living actors and actresses of the British stage. With criticisms from contemporary journals ” was well received by the Era (then London’s main theatrical journal) “As a work of reference for the actor or the playgoer it will be welcome...”. As James Ellis has noted, critical writing about the theatre, although produced in significant quantity during the mid-Victorian age, was largely ephemeral, rarely transitioning to book form, and certainly not systematically organised in the way that Pascoe’s work is. Documenting the “personations” and performances, and reviews of leading living actors and actresses was not an entirely novel idea, but Pascoe’s methodical treatment of the data is distinctive. Although the work remains an important resource for theatre historians to this day, it was not profitable enough to survive beyond its second edition. Instead, Pascoe returned to the more lucrative field of Guide Books targetting the swelling tide of American and Colonial visitors to London.

In the 1881 census, the Pascoe family resides at 2 Mayfield Villas, a recent development in Wandsworth. Pascoe is described as a “Retired Civil Servant and Author” with a wife, two children, and a domestic servant. Ten years later, in the 1891 Census, although Pascoe himself is missing for some reason, the household includes a third child and has moved to 89 Hopton Road, where they are renting a moderately sized semi-detached “villa” in a new development, located a few minutes walk from Streatham railway station in one direction and from Streatham Common in the other. In Wandsworth, the Pascoes had mixed with builders; but here they are in prime middle class country

The first edition of Pascoe’s guide book, “London of To-day” appeared in 1885, with a new and much revised edition every year thereafter until at least 1904. It elaborated considerably on the basic idea of his London directory for American travellers for 1874 -- rather than a simple assemblage of facts, the Guidebook embeds factual information in increasingly verbose discursive prose, which provides historical context and a very personal perspective. Mr Punch was an early fan (Punch, April 3, 1886):

It is an oddly self-conscious work, making much of those annual revisions. Early volumes are prefixed by defensive responses to negative criticism, alongside quotations from more positive reviews. The tone is earnest and friendly, inviting the reader's complicity with the authorial voice . The format facilitates a historical perspective, each annual volume noting for example what has changed in “Society” over the past year; at the same time, by focussing on the three main themes – where to stay; where to eat; and what to do – it suggests that little ever really changes. From about the 8th edition (1892), there is a focus on the Guide Book itself, in particular the extent to which it accurately represents the full richness and variety of “London To-Day”. In the name of comprehensiveness, the Guide Book becomes in its later editions a personal manifesto: Though originally planned solely as a guide to Visitors… in reality it is somewhat more. (1892, p.33)

Publication of these low priced and lavishly illustrated works was only financially viable because of the copious advertising they contain, much of it paid for by businesses also recommended in the text. Pascoe insists however that his recommendations derive entirely from his own direct experience during a 12 year long residence in the capital. He also frequently asserts that the Guide reflects the changing nature of the Metropolis and that his taste may not suit all visitors

A more substantial criticism perhaps is that the work necessarily distorts the real London of To-day. Forced to confront the chasm between rich and poor, Pascoe does no better or worse than any other Liberal, then or now. Anxieties about class, gender, and religion are never far from the surface. He celebrates what might now be regarded as “woke” efforts to improve the lot of the poor, while asserting repeatedly that the lower middle class is financially worse off and more heavily taxed than the true working class. Describing Derby Day in 1887 he asserts “Most race-meetings near London draw together as choice a collection of blackguards and vagabonds of every degree as anywhere congregate.; and yet in 1902, claims that “The vigorous and orderly good sense, and intelligence, and wholesome respect for the authority of the police, which in general characterises a great London crowd, or " mob " if you will, may be classed among the most astonishing and pleasing features of our times. (1902 p.224)

By the turn of the century, Pascoe was an established producer of guide books. Under the “London of Today” imprint he issued “pocket books” describing nearby resorts such as Brighton, Folkestone, or Hastings. With funding from local businesses and the railway companies, he produced pamphlets and at least two series of “Holiday Leaflets Illustrated” priced at one penny describing more exotic locations such as Cromer, Scarborough, or Skegness, thus contributing to their identification as suitable tourist destinations.

None of this however made him rich. We know this because in 1906, at the age of 64, he made an application for financial assistance to the Royal Literary Fund. Dated 22 September 1906, this makes rather depressing reading. Under the heading “Present means” he writes “None : Five years ago I had £500 in Bank now expended in supporting my home. I calculate that supporting myself and 3 others it has cost me £160 a year. I have earned less than £20”. The application is supported by two letters in Pascoe’s own barely legible hand, lamenting his inability to find work “the whole condition of publishing is changed. Journalism is changed. There is no longer any limit to literary working as a calling. The wealthy are at it. MPs do newspaper work for pay. Old staid honourable magazines are dead. The old editors are dead. All of which you know...” The committee of the Royal Literary Fund did not find this persuasive, and his application was rejected with the brief annotation “authorship insufficient”.

By this time, the Pascoe family had moved to a new home on Marchmont Rd, Wallington, and it was here in November 1912 that Pascoe died unexpectedly. According to the local press, his death was precipitated by the barking of a neighbour’s dog. Two local papers (the Sutton and Cheam Advertiser and the Croydon Guardian and Surrey County Gazette) covered the story in some detail, and nine other provincial papers gave summarized versions. There does not seem to have been any formal obituary in the national press, beyond brief and not entirely accurate statements in the Westminster Gazette and the Pall Mall Gazette (A well-known man of letters and a graceful versifier has passed away in the person of Mr. Charles Eyre Pascoe, who for many years was a familiar figure in Bohemian circles).

He left an estate valued at £88 15s 9d, alongside a collection of works tracking major changes in the history of London and the evolution of mass tourism. By exhaustively documenting how the traveller wished (or was thought to wish) to experience “England” as spectacle, he anticipates current notions of cultural heritage, yet his final publications also prefigure the modern “advertorial”. It is sad that his name seems to have disappeared from history as completely as the world he once inhabited and sought to describe.
